answer:
English is almost impossible to avoid in everyday life. We hear it on television and in song lyrics, study it at school, and, for many of us, use it at work. This constant exposure gives us a fairly good intuitive sense of how the language works. I think most people understand at least some English, and quite a few probably have an excellent command of it. However, when I consider my own abilities, it is clear that I find some aspects of the language more challenging than others. I feel more confident in the receptive skills—reading and listening—than in writing and speaking.

Throughout my years of studying English, from primary through upper secondary school, my teachers placed a strong emphasis on writing. In upper secondary school in particular, we wrote many essays and various kinds of reviews. Despite all this writing practice, I still encounter difficulties. Spelling can sometimes be challenging, but grammatical errors are a greater concern for me. In my experience, grammar problems are often complicated and difficult to resolve, unlike spelling mistakes, which can usually be corrected by looking up a word in a dictionary.

We did not get much reading practice at school. Although we had textbooks, the passages were often very short and covered unrelated topics, making them seem disconnected and out of context. In short, I found the textbooks boring. We also read several works of literature and wrote reviews of them. I think reading literature is a tremendously rewarding way to develop fluency in a language. This experience also helped me when I took courses in religious studies, as much of the required reading was in English.

My greatest difficulty when reading English is dealing with specialist language. A text that would be challenging even in Swedish becomes particularly demanding in English and can take a great deal of time to work through. This brings me to another problem: my patience, or rather, my lack of it. Naturally, reading in English takes longer than reading in Swedish, at least initially, but for some reason I find that difficult to accept.

Speaking and listening are obviously closely related, yet I find listening the easiest of the four language skills and speaking the hardest. This is undoubtedly because I get far more practice listening, especially through television and music, than speaking. Although I do not understand every word, I can usually follow the general meaning without difficulty. However, specialist language poses problems when I listen, just as it does when I read.

As I mentioned earlier, speaking is the aspect of English I struggle with most. I have had little experience of using English in everyday conversation, as I have never spent an extended period abroad. Since English teaching at school focused primarily, if not exclusively, on theory, I had little opportunity to practise speaking there either. If anything, school can make you even more reluctant to speak: you become so concerned about getting the grammar right that you dare not open your mouth for fear of being laughed at. I know this sounds rather bleak, and it probably does not apply to everyone. Nevertheless, I believe these fears would fade fairly quickly with regular speaking practice.

Having completed this assignment, I have realised how difficult it is to assess my own abilities in the four language skills. I never had any trouble getting good grades in English at school, but I firmly believe that grades rarely reflect what someone actually knows. What I do know is that learning a language involves many different skills, and I would like to develop all of them.
